CaseStudy.title: Digitising a company’s entire operation from scratch
CaseStudy.clientNote: Security netting and industrial textile manufacturing
problem: Sales and operations ran on separate tracks. Orders arrived by phone and WhatsApp, stock was tracked in hand-kept spreadsheets, and invoices were prepared somewhere else entirely.
The real cost of that setup was not mistakes but repetition: the same information was typed into three different places. Finding out where an order stood meant asking two or three people.
An off-the-shelf store or a boxed ERP did not fit the trade. Security netting is sold by square metre, weave type and custom dimensions — standard product-and-variant logic does not describe that.

approach.title: I learned the process before writing code
approach.body: The first job was following a single order all the way through the company. Which step waits on whom, where information gets lost. Most of the technical decisions came out of that map.

approach.title: One flow, not two systems bolted together
approach.body: Commerce and ERP are usually separate products with an integration layer between them. Here I designed both to face each other from the start: an order placed in the store is a record the ERP is already expecting.

approach.title: No compromise where the trade is specific
approach.body: Proforma invoicing, custom-dimension pricing and wholesale tiers are either missing from ready-made tools or awkwardly bolted on. Rather than force them into a generic shape, I wrote them as their own modules.

approach.title: A system someone else can take over
approach.body: The people using it are not developers. I built every screen on the assumption that someone would sit down at it for the first time without training; anywhere that needs explaining is a design failure.

results: Orders, stock, accounts and invoicing live in one panel. The same information is no longer entered by hand in several places.
Everyone sees their own work: separate panels for the owner, accounting, field staff and online sales.
Invoices, account statements and reference documents come out of the system itself rather than a separate program.
Barcode and QR scanning works in the warehouse, so stock counts and movements need no manual entry.
An order placed online lands directly in the panel and notifies the right person immediately.
Spreadsheet-and-paper tracking has moved into the system; the status of an order is visible from one place.

CaseStudyPeony.title: In second-hand luxury, the real problem is trust
problem: In second-hand luxury, both sides are nervous at the same time. The buyer cannot be sure a bag worth tens of thousands is genuine. The seller cannot be sure the money will arrive once the item is gone.

Because of that, these trades usually happen through acquaintances, in messaging apps, with cash changing hands. It does not scale, nothing is recorded, and when something goes wrong neither side has anything to fall back on.
So the problem to solve was never "build a website". It was to put trust inside the transaction itself.

approach.title: Verification inside the process, not beside it
approach.body: Authentication is not an add-on the buyer chases afterwards; it is a step the item must pass before it reaches them. The platform is built so a sale cannot complete on an unverified item.

approach.title: Hold the money so it protects both sides
approach.body: Payment is held until the buyer confirms the item. The buyer is not risking their money, and the seller is not left unpaid after shipping. Trust is not left to good intentions.

approach.title: Do not make sellers learn software
approach.body: Someone selling a handbag is not a software user. The consignment process was kept as simple as filling in a form, with the platform absorbing the work behind it.

approach.title: Never let technical decisions break the feeling of luxury
approach.body: In this segment the experience is part of the product. Getting the technical side right — from page speed to image quality — without disturbing how the brand feels was the invisible but decisive part of the job.

results: The purchase flow does not advance until authentication is complete.
Payment protection covers buyer and seller at the same time.
Sellers can list their own items; the process requires no technical knowledge.
The platform is live and serves as the brand’s sales channel.
